title: The SQL parser's DFA cache is unbounded unless Spark manages it
verdict: A large statement pins hundreds of MB of driver heap until `spark.sql.parser.manageParserCaches` is on
description: Spark parses SQL with ANTLR, whose DFA cache is static: it lives as long as the driver JVM and grows with every statement, the more for deeply nested ones. Spark 4.1 added its own cache management behind `spark.sql.parser.manageParserCaches` (internal, default false): with it on, `parserDfaCacheFlushThreshold` (a number of DFA states) or `parserDfaCacheFlushRatio` (a percentage of the driver's memory, about 9,700 bytes per state) flushes the cache after a parse that exceeds it. Both are -1, off, by default.

With the defaults, parsing the 51 kB statement sverify wrote for the coverage case `month end` (`ts.date().truncate("M") + 1 month - 1 day`, #821) took the live heap after a full GC from 469 MB to 863 MB of a 1 GB driver. It stayed there for the rest of the session: later queries failed with `[AGGREGATE_OUT_OF_MEMORY]` or "Not enough memory to build and broadcast the table", and the JVM ended in GC thrash. With `manageParserCaches=true` and `parserDfaCacheFlushRatio=10`, the same session stayed at about 100 MB, at most 154 MB over about 1,000 queries.
Results do not change: the failure is the query's, not a wrong answer. It shows only when one JVM parses many statements, as a long-lived session or a single-process test run does.
reference: The reference has no notion of a parser or of driver memory; a plan's result does not depend on the statements parsed before it.

provenance.checked_by: Spark OOM investigation for the 0.5.0 release (#816)

evidence.note: `parserDfaCacheFlushRatio`, `parserDfaCacheFlushThreshold` (both default -1) and `manageParserCaches` (default false); the threshold's doc says the cache has no limit and that large statements cause high GC overhead and eventually OOMs
the flush after a parse when the cache exceeds the threshold
`BYTES_PER_DFA_STATE = 9700`; Spark installs its own caches only when `manageParserCaches` is on

provenance.checked_by: Spark OOM investigation for the 0.5.0 release (#816), on homelab

evidence.note: Run with the `ci` profile in one process together with the Spark tests of `test_nodes.py` and `test_sql_spark.py`, as the Wheels `test-pythons` job runs them. Live heap after `System.gc()` before each query: 333 MB at query 129, 469 MB at 137, then 863 MB from 138 on: query 137 was the `month end` statement. Lowering `spark.sql.ui.retainedExecutions` to 10 or `spark.sql.codegen.cache.maxEntries` to 1, or a Python `gc.collect()`, left it at 860 MB; `manageParserCaches=true` with `parserDfaCacheFlushRatio=10` kept it near 100 MB.

Failed with `[AGGREGATE_OUT_OF_MEMORY]` in every Linux job of the v0.5.0 Wheels run (https://github.com/AlexanderNenninger/substrait-lean/actions/runs/42027728771) after `test_spark_agrees_with_duckdb` had parsed the statement in the same JVM.
`LOCAL_CONF` turns the management on for sverify's local session (#816).

provenance.notes: Spark 4.3.0 (pyspark 4.3.0), OpenJDK 21.0.12, Linux x86_64 (homelab), `local[2]`, default 1 GB driver. Open: the macOS jobs of the same Wheels run (macos-15, Python 3.13 and 3.15) and a macOS arm64 laptop (OpenJDK 21.0.13) ran the same tests in one process and passed; why the parse pinned less memory there is not known.
